item.title: CIS confab to rally capital mobilisation for infrastructure, manufacturing
item.description: By Yinka Kolawole Nigeria’s economic policymakers, financial market regulators, institutional investors and industry leaders will converge in Lagos on November 4 and 5 for the 30th Annual Conference of the Chartered Institute of Stockbrokers (CIS), with a focus on mobilising capital for productive investment and economic growth. The conference, scheduled to hold in Lagos, will examine how the capital market can translate funds raised into tangible economic outcomes, including business expansion, job creation and improved global competitiveness. With the theme, “From Capital Mobilised to Prosperity Realised: Financing Nigeria’s Next Era of Growth and Global Competitiveness”, the event is expected to provide a platform for stakeholders to develop practical solutions to the country’s investment and development challenges. President of CIS, Dr Fiona Ahimie, said the conference would provide an opportunity to rethink the role of the capital market in financing Nigeria’s economic transformation. She said the focus must shift from the volume of capital raised to its effective deployment in expanding productive capacity, creating jobs and strengthening businesses. “Our focus must go beyond mobilising capital to ensuring that capital translates into productive investment, business expansion, employment generation and shared prosperity. “Nigeria’s next phase of growth requires a capital market that is innovative, inclusive, efficient and competitive enough to attract both domestic and international investment,” Ahimie said. Chairman of the Conference Committee, Saheed Bashir, said the conference was designed to bring together key players across the investment value chain to develop actionable recommendations for financing Nigeria’s growth ambitions. He said discussions would examine the links between capital market development, technology, regulatory effectiveness and the financing needs of the real economy. “This conference is designed to move the conversation from the potential of the capital market to practical solutions that can finance businesses, accelerate infrastructure development, support manufacturing and unlock opportunities for small and medium-sized enterprises. We want the deliberations to produce ideas that policymakers, regulators, investors and industry leaders can translate into measurable outcomes,” Bashir said. A major session, titled “Financing Productive Investments in the Real Economy: Spotlight on Infrastructure, Manufacturing, and SMEs,” will examine ways to expand access to long-term financing for sectors critical to economic development. The session will explore how the capital market can complement bank lending by connecting businesses and infrastructure projects with long-term funding from institutional and other investors. item.title: Ifeanyi Okoye emerges 12th President of MAN
item.description: By Yinka Kolawole The Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN) has elected Dr. Ifeanyi Okoye, Chief Executive Officer of Juhel Nigeria Limited, as its 12th President . He succeeds Otunba Francis Meshioye, who completed his four-year tenure at the recently-concluded 54th Annual General Meeting of the association held on 7th October 2026 in Lagos. A statement by Director General of MAN, Segun Ajayi-Kadir, noted that Okoye holds a Bachelor’s degree in Pharmacy from the University of Ife (now Obafemi Awolowo University) with a Bachelor’s degree in Pharmacy and an M.Sc. and PhD in Pharmaceutical Technology and Industrial Pharmacy from the University of Nigeria, Nsukka, graduating as the best student in his class. He established JUHEL Nigeria Limited in 1987, a wholly indigenous pharmaceutical manufacturing company with headquarters in Enugu, Enugu State, and moved to its permanent site in Emene, Enugu, in 2001 with facilities expanded to include syrups and capsules. In 2010, JUHEL opened a major parenteral manufacturing facility in Awka, Anambra State. Okoye is a Fellow of the Pharmaceutical Society of Nigeria and an alumnus of Harvard Business School in Boston, USA. He attended the National Institute for Policy and Strategic Studies in Kuru, Plateau State, and was conferred the national honour of Officer of the Order of the Federal Republic (OFR) in 2012. He has served on several committees, including the Ministerial Committee on the Establishment of World-Class Hospitals and Diagnostic Centers from 2013 to 2015; Member of the Governing Council of the Standard Organization of Nigeria (SON) – 2009 to 2022. Before he was elected President, Okoye served MAN in various capacities, including as Chairman of the Enugu, Anambra and Ebonyi States Branches from 1998 to 2005, and as Vice President from 2006 to 2010. item.description: The Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Prof Ali Pate, has disclosed that the Swiss authorities have confirmed the safe arrival of Nigeria’s Ebola index patient and her spouse in Switzerland. Pate, in an update on his X handle on Monday evening, noted that the patient is now receiving treatment at Geneva University Hospitals, while her husband has been placed in isolation at University Hospital Zurich. According to him, contact monitoring, investigation of alerts and other containment measures were continuing in Nigeria. “The Swiss authorities have confirmed that the patient and her spouse arrived safely in Switzerland today,” Pate stated. item.title: Dollar to Naira exchange rate today, October 27, 2026
item.description: Trading in Nigeria’s foreign exchange market opened with the local currency displaying subtle fluctuations against the United States dollar across both official and unofficial channels. At the official Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM), the naira opened around N1,339.93 to the dollar, reflecting minor adjustments during early morning trading. This follows recent sessions where the official rate navigated pressure from elevated dollar demand, lingering near the N1,330 to N1,360 threshold. In the parallel market, currency operators in major hubs like Lagos and Abuja continue to quote wider spreads due to immediate liquidity needs. Independent dealers reported buying rates floating around N1,370 per dollar, while selling rates averaged between N1,380 and N1,385 per dollar. Market participants note that overall liquidity conditions remain tied to foreign capital inflows and central bank intervention strategies. Although foreign reserves maintain a stable buffer above $55 billion, ongoing demand from importers and domestic businesses keeps pressure steady across all FX segments. item.title: FG launches trade intelligence tools to boost exports, investment
item.description: By Yinka Kolawole The Federal Government has launched new trade intelligence tools to help Nigerian businesses access international markets, attract productive investments and strengthen local industries’ competitiveness as part of efforts to build a $1 trillion economy by 2030. Minister of Industry, Trade and Investment, Dr Jumoke Oduwole, who unveiled the initiative in Abuja, said the tools would provide exporters and investors with reliable market information to guide business decisions, navigate trade requirements and translate economic reforms into industrial growth and job creation. Oduwole said Nigeria had recorded significant progress in capital inflows and non-oil exports, but stressed the need to convert the gains into productive investments, completed export transactions and stronger domestic industries. She disclosed that capital importation rose from about $3.9 billion in 2023 to more than $23 billion in 2025, while non-oil exports reached a record N12.36 trillion, with Nigerian products gaining access to more than 120 countries. The minister also said intra-African trade grew by 21 per cent in 2025, describing the development as an opportunity for Nigeria to expand its participation in regional and global markets. However, she acknowledged that businesses continued to face high production costs, limited access to finance, logistics constraints and complex trade procedures. According to her, the new tools would help exporters identify promising markets, understand applicable tariffs and entry requirements, and obtain credible information before shipping their products. Oduwole identified the forthcoming CANEX Weekend 2026 and the Intra-African Trade Fair 2027, both strategic platforms for promoting Nigerian products and connecting businesses with international buyers and investors, as key opportunities to expand trade. She announced that the ministry planned to formally launch its Trade Portal at CANEX Weekend, scheduled for November 5 to 8, 2026. The portal is expected to provide businesses with market intelligence and help convert trade contacts into actual commercial transactions. Meanwhile, President of the Nigerian Association of Chambers of Commerce, Industry, Mines and Agriculture, NACCIMA, Jani Ibrahim, called for increased private-sector investment in value-added exports, competitive manufacturing and priority export value chains. Ibrahim said such investments would improve the global competitiveness of Nigerian products, increase domestic value addition and create more jobs. He stressed the importance of strengthening local industries to enable Nigeria to take greater advantage of emerging opportunities in regional and international markets. item.title: BoI secures €2.22bn, N250bn funding for Nigerian industries
item.description: By Yinka Kolawole The Bank of Industry (BoI) has secured more than €2.22 billion and N250 billion in new funding through major financing transactions concluded between 2024 and 2026, as the development finance institution intensifies efforts to bridge Nigeria’s industrial financing gap. Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of BoI, Dr. Olasupo Olusi, disclosed this at a media roundtable, highlighting the bank’s capital mobilisation drive as a key pillar of its 2025–2027 corporate strategy. The transactions include a €1.879 billion syndicated facility secured in 2024, €210 million raised from international development partners in 2025, and a N250 billion development bond issued in 2026, which was oversubscribed. The bank also secured €85 million from the European Investment Bank (EIB) in 2026 to support agriculture, alongside another €50 million facility from the European lender for healthcare manufacturing. Olusi said the funding transactions reflected growing investor confidence in the bank’s governance, financing pipeline and development impact. “Nigerian businesses need long-term, affordable capital, and the commercial banking system cannot provide enough of it. Filling that gap is our job,” he said. He added: “Investors have placed this money with us because they trust our governance, our pipeline and our results.” The €1.879 billion syndicated facility, concluded in 2024, was subsequently recognised as Syndicated Loan Deal of the Year, while the oversubscription of the N250 billion development bond underscored investor appetite for the bank’s industrial financing activities. The EIB facilities are expected to strengthen financing for domestic agricultural production and healthcare manufacturing, supporting efforts to reduce Nigeria’s dependence on imported food and medicines. Olusi said the capital-raising drive was central to the bank’s ambition to spearhead sustainable and inclusive industrial development, with particular attention to manufacturing, infrastructure and underserved businesses. Under its 2025–2027 corporate strategy, BoI aims to double its loan book, disbursements and development impact instruments within three years. The bank has prioritised 15 sectors grouped under agro-manufacturing, other manufacturing, infrastructure, extractive industries and services. item.title: FBI arrests 9 Nigerians, tracks $11m in fresh fraud crackdown — US Mission
item.description: By Nkiruka Nnorom & Marvellous Chukwunenye The United States Mission in Nigeria has announced a major breakthrough in the fight against transnational cybercrime, with the Federal Bureau of Investigation, FBI, arresting nine suspects in Nigeria in an operation targeting scam centres stealing billions of dollars from Americans. FBI Director, Kash Patel, disclosed this in a post on X which was reposted by the US Mission in Nigeria, saying the operation, code-named Operation Blackout, is taking the fight directly to international cybercriminal networks. According to Patel, the Nigeria operation delivered nine arrests, seizure of 53 electronic devices and identification of $11 million in potentially freezable funds across multiple countries. “Operation Blackout is taking the fight directly to the international cybercriminal networks stealing billions from Americans,” Patel said. “These scam centers exploit innocent victims, steal life savings, and operate across international borders believing they are beyond the reach of law enforcement. They’re wrong,” he stated. He commended Nigerian law enforcement and partners in London for their cooperation. “Thanks to Nigerian law enforcement and our partners in London for their outstanding cooperation,” Patel said, warning: “To the criminals targeting Americans from overseas: Justice will fibd you.” While the FBI did not name the Nigerian agency involved or the locations of the arrests, the operation is part of a wider international enforcement exercise coordinated from London. According to the US Department of Justice, the broader crackdown resulted in 28 arrests across Nigeria and Ghana and the seizure of hundreds of electronic devices. The operation also involved Meta and 14 other technology companies, leading to the removal of more than 3.7 million fraudulent accounts, pages and groups linked to West African scam networks. Reports indicate that 19 of the arrests were made in Ghana, where 117 victims, said to have been trafficked and forced to work in a residential compound running scam operations, are pending repatriation to Nigeria. The arrests come amid heightened US-Nigeria cooperation on cybercrime. This is the central purpose of NES #32. “Nigeria’s recent reforms, including petrol subsidy removal, foreign exchange liberalisation, fiscal restructuring, tax reforms and recapitalisation of the banking sector, represent significant changes to our economic policy framework. “These measures were necessary to address distortions that weakened public finances and constrained the efficient allocation of resources. “However, stabilisation creates the conditions for progress; it does not automatically deliver it. For instance, a more stable exchange rate does not, by itself, make a manufacturer competitive. “For households, reform must mean decent jobs, greater purchasing power, improved security and reduced poverty. “For businesses, it must mean lower production costs, reliable infrastructure, including power, higher productivity and affordable financing.” Yusuf also outlined the focus of the 2026 NESG under the theme, “Growth that Works: Delivering Jobs, Productivity and Shared Prosperity,” saying it expresses a fundamental proposition: economic growth must create value, expand opportunity and improve lives. He stated: “GDP growth alone cannot tell us whether enterprises are becoming more competitive or households are better off. We must judge success by the quality of jobs, the productivity of businesses and how widely prosperity reaches our people. “Three interdependent priorities guide this Summit: Productivity, which asks how to reduce production costs, optimise outputs and strengthen competitiveness; Human Capital, which asks how to invest in education, healthcare, nutrition and skills; and Resilience, which asks how to help households and businesses withstand shocks. “These three priorities reinforce one another. Yet they cannot fulfil this role without an enabling operating environment. “Our entrepreneurs are remarkably resilient, but resilience should not excuse an environment that makes productivity unnecessarily expensive. “Unreliable electricity, expensive financing, poor transport infrastructure, insecurity and regulatory uncertainty raise costs and increase volatility, especially for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. “The government must sustain economic stability, provide essential public goods and ensure regulatory predictability. Campaigns for the Presidential and National Assembly polls opened on August 19. By then, several states had already published fee schedules, and the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, had cleared 19 presidential candidates. Abia sets the highest rate. Its signage agency charges N200 million for a presidential candidate, N150 million for a governorship candidate, N100 million for a senatorial candidate, N50 million for the House of Representatives and N20 million for the State Assembly. Enugu and Kogi each demand N150 million from presidential candidates. Cross River is reported at N150 million, Rivers at N75 million and Anambra at N50 million, a five-fold rise on its 2022 presidential fee of N10 million. The contrast with other states shows how arbitrary the figures are. Kano charges about N1.15 million and draws no distinction between political and commercial billboards. Kaduna assesses fees site by site. Imo asks senatorial candidates for N5 million, plus application and inspection charges. A question of arithmetic The sums matter because of the spending ceiling in the Electoral Act 2026, which caps a presidential candidate’s election expenses at N10 billion and a governorship candidate’s at N3 billion. If Abia’s N200 million applied in all 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, permits alone would cost N7.4 billion, or 74 per cent of the presidential cap, before a single rally, jingle or vehicle is paid for. The Allied Peoples Movement, APM, and its presidential candidate, Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde, argue that such fees could consume more than 80 per cent of the ceiling. They have asked the Abia High Court in suit HC/214/2026 to declare the N200 million fee unconstitutional and void. No hearing date had been announced at the last report, and no court has ruled on the legality of any of these fees. Not simply an APC tyranny The opposition has described the fees as a ruling-party tactic. The African Democratic Congress, ADC, said they are targeted at the opposition and has vowed to challenge them. The Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, said the states involved are mostly controlled by the All Progressives Congress, APC. But the record is more complicated. The N200 million fee in Abia was imposed by the administration of Governor Alex Otti of the Labour Party, LP. In Oyo, the APC accuses the APM-led state government of directing its signage agency to clamp down on non-APM campaigners. Enugu and Kogi, both APC-controlled, are among the states where the opposition’s complaints are sharpest. That cuts both ways. It weakens the claim of a single party’s master plan, but it strengthens the broader point that incumbent governments in several parties now control the gate to public advertising space. What the states say Governments insist the charges are administrative. Abia says its schedule applies to every party and that it “will not discriminate against any political party or any candidate.” Kogi State Information Commissioner, Kingsley Fanwo, said the rules bind APC candidates as well, adding that “the government is for everybody.” Enugu’s APC says it is paying the fee itself. The states cite their powers over physical planning and urban aesthetics, and Abia says a billboard collapse in Aba in 2025 informed its approach. Critics are not persuaded. A political scientist at Bayero University, Kano, Prof. Kamilu Sani Fage, argues that ruling parties will probably pay with public funds, while opposition candidates pay from their own pockets. Abia’s opposition, the ADC and the PDP, also question whether state agencies have the power to levy these fees at all. For Prof. Fage, the timing is the problem. “It is wrong to introduce such measures now,” he said. The Out-of-Home Advertising Association of Nigeria wants states to keep to gazetted tariffs. The Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria, ARCON, has said state agencies have no authority to approve political adverts before they are displayed. Legal gap The Electoral Act is silent on billboard placement, leaving it to state and local laws, according to a constitutional lawyer, Kehinde Oloje. That gap is what states are using. Opponents point to the Act’s prohibition on using state apparatus to favour or disadvantage any candidate to the spending cap, and to the constitutional rights to free expression and association in sections 39 and 40. However, states are relying on their Land Use Act powers, even though there are arguments that outdoor advertising fees should be collected by local councils. Early effects The impact is already visible. In Lagos, where the signage agency’s rates are not campaign-specific, many opposition candidates had not placed any signboard since campaigns opened. In Imo, the Action People’s Party, APP, says it is paying even though the charges are high. In Abia, the APC governorship candidate, Eric Opah, says “workers, pensioners and traders” will be his billboards rather than paid-space. The shift matters because billboards are cheap per exposure and durable, which is why politicians favour them. Candidates who cannot afford them are left with radio (especially the private ones), social media and town halls. Way forward Stakeholders are asking INEC to issue guidelines separating administrative fees from campaign expenses, and the National Assembly to cap state levies on political advertising. They want states to publish who has paid and who has been waived, and the courts to rule early enough on the matter. INEC’s chairman, Prof. Joash Amupitan SAN, has said the commission will track illegal campaign spending and that broadcasters must give all parties equal access. item.title: NESG: We’re rewriting Nigeria’s story of under-performance — Tinubu
item.description: By Johnbosco Agbakwuru ABUJA — President Bola Tinubu said yesterday that his administration is rewriting Nigeria’s decades-long story of economic under-performance through far-reaching reforms designed to dismantle structural barriers, unlock the nation’s enormous potential and deliver jobs, productivity and shared prosperity. He also said the administration is currently undertaking what it came into office to achieve — rewriting the story of a nation that had performed below its potential for far too long. Speaking when he formally declared open the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit Group, NESG, in Abuja yesterday, President Tinubu, who was represented by Vice President Kashim Shettima, noted that his administration began on a difficult note because there was no shortcut to economic growth. “We came to rewrite the story of a nation that has performed below its potential for far too long. But there is no shortcut to economic growth. This is why we began with a difficult reset. For us, rescuing the economy means rescuing livelihoods and transforming the fortunes of young job seekers, farmers, manufacturers, entrepreneurs and innovators. “We cannot harness the immense opportunities offered by our growing population without first stabilising the economy. He also said the administration is currently undertaking what it came into office to achieve — rewriting the story of a nation that had performed below its potential for far too long. Speaking when he formally declared open the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit Group, NESG, in Abuja yesterday, President Tinubu, who was represented by Vice President Kashim Shettima, noted that his administration began on a difficult note because there was no shortcut to economic growth. “We came to rewrite the story of a nation that has performed below its potential for far too long. But there is no shortcut to economic growth. This is why we began with a difficult reset. For us, rescuing the economy means rescuing livelihoods and transforming the fortunes of young job seekers, farmers, manufacturers, entrepreneurs and innovators. “We cannot harness the immense opportunities offered by our growing population without first stabilising the economy. We must also create the conditions for the public and private sectors to invest, expand and generate productive employment,” he explained. Tinubu observed that the summit’s theme, “Growth That Works: Delivering Jobs, Productivity and Shared Prosperity,” was built on the ambition of the previous edition of the annual event to achieve a prosperous and inclusive Nigeria by 2030. He noted that his administration had “since set in motion a series of reforms to dismantle the structural barriers that have prevented our abundant human and natural resources from yielding prosperity. “These reforms are restoring confidence, strengthening our economic foundations and laying the groundwork for sustainable growth.” The President noted that the administration was encouraged by what it had accomplished so far, acknowledging that creating jobs was only half the task. ‘Need to improve quality of work’ While noting there is need to improve the quality of work, reduce underemployment and harness the potential of the country’s under-utilised workforce, Tinubu said: “Our pursuit of prosperity demands greater productivity from every worker, enterprise and investment. There is some force in that argument. A governor who is expected to answer questions about the safety of residents should have an effective means of contributing to the security of those residents. But responsibility without control is only one side of the problem. The other is control without accountability. A governor is not a neutral administrator standing outside politics. He belongs to a political party, has political allies and opponents, and may be interested in securing the election of a preferred successor. If a state police structure becomes too dependent on the governor for appointments, promotions, discipline, funding or operational direction, the distinction between public security and partisan interest could become dangerously blurred. Consider what could happen when an election approaches. An opposition party announces a rally in a town where the ruling party fears losing support. An opposition candidate plans to visit a community to discuss unemployment, abandoned projects or allegations of poor governance. Young people organise a peaceful protest against government policy. In each instance, the police should protect lawful activity and enforce the law impartially. But what happens if the officers believe their careers depend on pleasing the governor? Could a lawful political meeting be subjected to unnecessary restrictions? Could police powers be used selectively against opposition organisers while supporters of the ruling party enjoy greater freedom? Could citizens become afraid to express political preferences because they fear the consequences? These are risks that Nigeria cannot afford to dismiss as hypothetical inconveniences. They go to the heart of democratic competition. The danger is particularly serious as the country approaches the 2027 general elections. Establishing a new police structure involves recruitment, training, funding, command arrangements, jurisdictional rules and mechanisms for investigating misconduct. These are not matters that should be hurried through simply to demonstrate political determination. A poorly prepared transition could create confusion among security agencies at the very time Nigerians need impartial and coordinated policing. There is a strong argument, therefore, for completing the legal and institutional groundwork now while deferring the operational deployment of state police until after the 2027 general elections. Such a transition should be carefully planned, consistent with the law and without weakening existing security operations. The objective would not be to abandon reform but to prevent a major change in the control of armed law-enforcement institutions from becoming entangled in an imminent electoral contest. This concern has already entered the national debate. In June 2026, Peter Obi called for the implementation of state police to be deferred until after the 2027 elections, citing concerns about political manipulation and the need for independent oversight. Omoyele Sowore made a similar call in August. Allegations of partisan policing have arisen under the present arrangement as well. Centralisation does not automatically guarantee neutrality, just as decentralisation does not automatically guarantee accountability. There is a significant difference between hearing someone talk about a place and seeing it with your own eyes,” he said. He said such opportunities were particularly valuable for people studying Russian language and said that TASS is working to organise more similar programmes. “I believe that we can continue this work in the future, enabling you to learn more about Russia and our country’s current situation,” he said. Kuzovnikov said with 122 years of history, TASS is ready to share its knowledge through educational programmes covering artificial intelligence, fact-checking and data management. item.title: NYSC, UNN disowned ex-minister Uche Nnaji’s certificates, ICPC witness tells court
item.description: An investigator with the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC), Yakubu Ibrahim, on Monday, told a Federal High Court in Abuja that both the University of Nigeria (UNN) and the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) disowned the degree and discharge certificates presented by former Minister of Innovation, Science and Technology, Uche Nnaji, to the Senate for his ministerial screening in 2023. The witness, Suprintendent of Police, Yakubu Ibrahim, testified as the first prosecution witness in the trial of Nnaji, who is facing a six-count charge marked FHC/ABJ/CR/389/2026, bordering on alleged corruption, fraud, conferring corrupt advantage and providing false information through the alleged presentation of forged university degree and national service certificates. item.content:encoded: An investigator with the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC), Yakubu Ibrahim, on Monday, told a Federal High Court in Abuja that both the University of Nigeria (UNN) and the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) disowned the degree and discharge certificates presented by former Minister of Innovation, Science and Technology, Uche Nnaji, to the Senate for his ministerial screening in 2023. The witness, Suprintendent of Police, Yakubu Ibrahim, testified as the first prosecution witness in the trial of Nnaji, who is facing a six-count charge marked FHC/ABJ/CR/389/2026, bordering on alleged corruption, fraud, conferring corrupt advantage and providing false information through the alleged presentation of forged university degree and national service certificates. The investigator, who was led in evidence by the prosecution counsel, J. A. Mumini (SAN), said he was part of the ICPC team that investigated two petitions against the defendant. The witness said his team was assigned to investigate the matter after the commission received two separate petitions alleging certificate forgery against Nnaji. He said the Chairman of the Special Task Force directed an investigation, prompting the commission to request relevant documents from the National Assembly, the Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF), University of Nigeria, Nsukka and the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC). He told the court that the team wrote to UNN to authenticate the Bachelor of Science certificate in Microbiology/Biochemistry allegedly submitted by Nnaji to the Senate. According to him, the university responded that it did not issue the certificate to the governorship candidate of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in Enugu for the 2027 election. The witness added that the team also contacted the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) over a discharge certificate 15th May 1986, but the NYSC equally disowned it, maintaining that it did not issue any such certificate to the ex-minister. Ibrahim further told the court that UNN supplied the investigators with the defendant’s academic records, including a notice of withdrawal issued over his failure to obtain the required grade in a course. When shown copies of the correspondence between the ICPC and the two institutions, the witness identified the documents, following which the prosecution sought to tender them in evidence. Defence counsel, Wole Olanipekun (SAN), said he would allow the documents to be admitted at that stage but reserve his objection until later. On the steps taken to interview the defendant, Ibrahim said the head of his section issued an invitation, but investigators could not locate his address. He said a copy of the invitation, dated May 5, 2026, was subsequently sent to the defendant’s email address and WhatsApp number. According to the witness, after Nnaji failed to honour the invitation, the ICPC liaised with the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) to effect his arrest on July 1. He added that the defendant was questioned and made statements dated July 1 and 2. During cross-examination by Olanipekun, the witness admitted that he did not visit UNN during the investigation and did not know the faculty to which the defendant had been admitted. He, however, said members of the investigating team interviewed the university’s Registrar. Asked whether the team established where the alleged certificates were forged, Ibrahim said he did not know. He also said the defendant made no comment on the allegations when questioned by investigators. On whether the team investigated where Nnaji undertook his national service, the witness said it did not because the NYSC had stated that it did not issue the certificate. “The NYSC said the certificate was not issued by it, which was why we didn’t inquire where he served,” he told the court. The witness also confirmed seeing a notice of withdrawal supplied by UNN. When asked to identify it, he identified the document, marked Exhibit C, dated November 7, 1984. He said the university explained in its letter the policy governing the grades required for the award of a certificate saying if one failed four times, the person was not qualified. Ibrahim said Nnaji failed at two stages and did not write the examination at the third stage for medical reasons. “The witness said, “the defendant went ahead to write the supplementary examination for which he did not register.” Ibrahim further testified that UNN confirmed that the BSc certificate in Microbiology and Biochemistry attributed to the defendant was not issued by the university.
